title: Session fragment coalescer and GPU-resident prefetch for microcache reuse
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Problem: Our current continuous-batching path sees substantial redundant attention-key/value work across closely related requests (same session or sub-session reuse). Recomputing similar KV segments repeatedly wastes GPU DRAM and increases p99 latency for small interactive workloads. Goal: reduce redundant KV residency and decoding work by coalescing small, recent request fragments into compact, content-addressed micro-fragments and lazily prefetching a small set of GPU-resident fragments that cover the next expected requests.
design_summary: We will introduce a Session Fragment Coalescer (SFC) that runs at the batching ingress and emits content-addressed micro-fragments (caf) keyed by a compact rolling fingerprint (64-bit). Fragments are stored in a two-tier store: a compact CPU-resident fragment index and a thin GPU resident slab that holds fully materialized KV slices for top-ranked hot fragments. The admission policy is tenant-affine and frequency-weighted (LRU with crediting). A probabilistic Bloom frontier reduces duplicate fragment inserts in the hot slab. Prefetch hints are generated from the scheduler's microbatch plan: when a request is admitted, the SFC scores candidate fragments for the session's predicted follow-ups and issues a lazy rehydrate request to the hot slab. Rehydration is cooperative: the serving runtime only copies fragments to GPU memory when the predicted reuse score exceeds a threshold and GPU memory headroom is available. If headroom is tight, fallback uses compact CPU fragments with on-demand expansion into ephemeral GPU buffers for single-request execution.
technical_decisions: 1) Use 64-bit rolling fingerprint (SipHash variant) for fragment identity to balance collision risk and storage. 2) Two-tier store (CPU index + GPU slab) avoids keeping large cold fragments resident. 3) Prefetch scoring uses a simple Markov predictor (session bigram of fragment transitions) initially; we may replace with a lightweight neural predictor after rollout. 4) Eviction uses crediting: fragments earn credits by serving repeat requests; background decay reduces stale fragment residency. 5) Avoid per-tenant hard isolation for the hot slab initially; implement soft-affinity with tenant credits to prevent noisy neighbors. 6) Maintain backward-compatible runtime API: no changes to public generation API; this is purely a runtime optimization layer.
performance_target: Microbenchmarks: reduce aggregate token work by 18-30% for interactive session workloads (median). End-to-end p99 latency target improvement of 25% on small-session traces (<=512 tokens), cost per response down 12% measured by GPU time. Memory: keep additional GPU slab usage under 3GB per serving instance on typical load; allow scaling knob in console.
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (canary): instrumented build behind feature flag on 5% of canary fleet. Collect reuse hit-rate, false-positive rehydrates, eviction churn, and p99 latency. Phase 1 (regional canary): 25% of traffic in US-west on runtime-1.21. Phase 2 (gradual): 100% of dev Tier workloads after 4 weeks of stable metrics. Phase 3: enable for Dedicated pools as opt-in via console. Each phase gated by safety metrics (error rate, memory OOMs, tail latency regression threshold).
testing_and_validation: - Unit tests for fingerprinting, admission/ejection, and bloom-frontier semantics. - Integration tests with continuous batching harness that simulates interleaved sessions and tenant mixes. - Load test in perf lab: replay 24h of production session traces with and without SFC; capture p50/p95/p99 latencies and GPU memory graphs. - Canary dashboards: fragment hit-rate, rehydrate latency, eviction rate, tenant fairness score. - Chaos tests: force GPU OOM simulation and verify fallback to CPU fragment path without request failures.
migration_and_backwards_compatibility: Transparent to callers. Running instances can enable/disable SFC without client changes. The runtime must tolerate mixed instances (some with SFC enabled in the routing pool). Rolling restarts are safe; eviction state is transient and not required for correctness.
tradeoffs_and_risks: - Risk: overaggressive prefetch increases GPU memory pressure and could harm throughput. Mitigation: conservative default thresholds, dynamic headroom gating, and automatic disable if OOM trends detected. - Risk: fingerprint collisions leading to incorrect reuse; collision rate acceptable for 64-bit but will monitor and raise to 128-bit if needed. - Risk: tenant fairness concerns; will implement credit windows and tenant penalties for noisy neighbors in Phase 2.
open_questions: - Should we persist fragment index checkpoints across instance restarts to speed warmup? (cost vs complexity) - What is the best default decay rate for credits across very bursty tenants? - When to switch to a learned predictor versus simple Markov?
